final_proof:
Let K be a subfield of ℂ, and denote its multiplicative identity by 1_K. First, 1_K is the same element as the multiplicative identity 1 of ℂ. Indeed, if this equality is included in the definition of subfield, there is nothing to prove. Even without that convention, the multiplication on K is the restriction of that on ℂ, so 1_K² = 1_K in ℂ. Hence 1_K(1_K − 1) = 0. Since 1_K is nonzero and ℂ is a field, it follows that 1_K − 1 = 0, and therefore 1_K = 1.

For a positive integer n, write n·1_K for the sum of n copies of 1_K. Because the addition on K is the restriction of complex addition and 1_K = 1, we have

n·1_K = 1 + ⋯ + 1 = n,

where the expression on the right is the usual complex number corresponding to the positive integer n. This complex number is nonzero because it is the positive real number n. Consequently, there is no positive integer n for which n·1_K = 0.

By definition, the characteristic of a field is the least positive integer n satisfying n·1_K = 0, if such an integer exists, and is 0 if no such positive integer exists. Thus char(K) = 0. Since K was an arbitrary subfield of ℂ, every subfield of ℂ has characteristic 0.
